parole.testo: Borrowed from German Akkuratesse, from (or influenced by) Italian accuratezza.

parole.significato: to be in straining pain, to suffer miserably
parole.testo: Borrowed from German krepieren, itself from Italian crepare. Attested since at least 1824.

parole.significato: prank, trick, a strange, silly or deceptive action
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fratze, from Italian frasca.

parole.significato: a giraffe, mammal of the genus Giraffa
parole.testo: From German Giraffe, from Middle High German geraff, seraffe, schraffe, from Italian giraffa, from Arabic زَرَافَة (zarāfa).
Borrowed from German Kartätsche, from Italian cartuccia, derived from Latin carta.
From German legieren, from Italian legare.

parole.significato: operetta, comic opera (light-hearted opera with spoken sections)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Operette, from Italian operetta.

parole.significato: food supplies, edible provision, in particular when travelling
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Proviant, in turn borrowed from Italian provianda.

Borrowed from German Rakete, from Italian rocchetta, from rochetto (“rocket”, literally “a bobbin”), diminutive of rocca (“a distaff”), of Germanic origin, perhaps Gothic rukka, from Proto-Germanic *rukkô (“a distaff, a staff with flax fibres tied loosely to it, used in spinning thread”). parole.significato: splits (move in dance or gymnastics in which the legs are extended straight out and perpendicular to the body)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Spagat, from Italian spaccata.

parole.significato: prank, caper, antic (strange, excessive or frivolous action)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Strapaze (“strain, hassle”), from Italian strapazzo. The contemporary sense developed in the phrase strapatsen maken, originally “to cause hassle” and then by extension “to behave strangely, act out”.
